flawed_step: 0012: The proof assumes that relaxing (v,u) during pass k+1 uses v's distance from before that pass. In an in-place Bellman–Ford implementation, dist[v] may already have been improved earlier in the same pass, so the resulting path can have more than k+1 edges.
counterexample: Let the vertices be s, a, u, with directed weighted edges (s,a) of weight 0, (a,u) of weight 0, and (s,u) of weight 10. Initialize dist[s]=0 and dist[a]=dist[u]=infinity. In the first full pass, process the edges in the order (s,a), (a,u), (s,u). Relaxing (s,a) sets dist[a]=0. Relaxing (a,u) then sets dist[u]=0 using the two-edge path s->a->u. Relaxing (s,u) leaves dist[u]=0. Thus after one pass dist[u]=0, although the smallest length of any s-to-u path having at most one edge is 10. Hence the stated lemma, and the inference in step 0012, fail for ordinary in-place relaxations.
assessment_summary: The base case is correct, but the induction step ignores cascading updates within one pass. The claimed equality would hold with synchronized copies of the previous pass's distances; ordinary in-place Bellman–Ford provides only the usual shortest-path correctness guarantee, not this exact edge-count equality after every pass.
